source.title: RATT: Leveraging Unlabeled Data to Guarantee Generalization
source.authors: S. Garg; Sivaraman Balakrishnan; J. Kolter; Zachary Chase Lipton

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material are present; no apparent cutoff or garbling that prevents reading the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: Tests generalization in a distinct setting: training with clean data augmented by randomly labeled examples, including changes to early stopping and weight decay. It does not directly test the mapped claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test performance and bounds for clean test data after adding randomly labeled training data. It does not report held-out accuracy on random labels, and its results on early stopping and weight decay are not dropout comparisons. Cited findings from prior work are not extracted.
record.test_reason: Table 1 tests V3 in a new setting: ResNet-18 and fully connected MLPs trained from scratch with momentum SGD on clean image data augmented with random labels. ResNet has higher clean test accuracy on both MNIST and CIFAR-10. The record incorrectly treats these architecture comparisons as unrelated to every version.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly correct: RATT provides post-training generalization bounds using added randomly labeled data, with empirical bounds tracking clean test performance before interpolation. Clarify that the deep-network guarantee requires Assumption 1, and that Table 1 reports only the dominating bound term: the full multiclass accuracy guarantees are 30.7 percentage points lower. Thus the displayed multiclass predictions should not themselves be described as tight full bounds.
record.recipe_differences: Adds randomly labeled examples to clean training data and evaluates a post-training bound; studies early stopping and weight decay as ways to retain performance and avoid fitting the added labels.
record.method_sensitivity: In the wide-network binary MNIST experiment, adding random-label data hurt unseen clean performance without early stopping or weight decay; with either, the performance difference was close to zero. The paper also reports that bounds become vacuous when training interpolates the data.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding randomly labeled examples hurts clean test performance in wide binary-MNIST networks trained to interpolation; early stopping or weight decay makes the penalty nearly zero.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The clean-test penalty from adding random-label data depends on whether training is regularized or stopped before interpolation.

fits_no_version.finding: RATT uses fit on randomly labeled training examples to estimate clean population performance; its guarantees become vacuous at interpolation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Poor fit to added random labels can provide post-training generalization guarantees under the paper's stated assumptions.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 139, 2021
record.problems: The deep-learning extension relies on Assumption 1, which the authors say is not guaranteed a priori. Several results are figure-only or described qualitatively, and Table 1 gives test accuracy without uncertainty estimates. The paper notes that CIFAR100 bounds are vacuous.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible version-specific results were found. The paper's oracle-bound curves in Appendix C are figure-only and concern a bound using underlying true labels for randomly labeled data, rather than a mapped claim version.

untested.parts: No matched natural-label versus entirely random-label training experiment with random-label held-out accuracy.
No width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.

Does not isolate local connectivity, learn sparse local connections in fully connected networks, or initialize fully connected networks from trained convolutional networks. No usable convolutional-versus-fully-connected comparison on CIFAR-100 or SVHN.
No controlled adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparison.
No batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
No dropout comparison or joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurements or ranking of generalization measures.
No removal of examples selected by memorization influence.

record.verdict_notes: The architecture comparisons support V3 despite serving as evaluations of RATT. They do not isolate which architectural feature causes the advantage. All judgments use only the supplied text; numerical trajectories cannot be recovered from its figure extraction.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare held-out performance after training on natural labels alone versus fixed random labels, or report held-out accuracy on random labels.
No width sweep beyond the width required for zero training error.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected architectures under the conditions in the version.
No controlled comparison of adaptive optimizers and SGD on the mapped benchmarks.
No large-batch versus small-batch comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
Does not test dropout or its interaction with data augmentation.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare it with other generalization measures.
Does not remove memorized examples and measure the effect on test accuracy.

rows.subject: MLP
rows.operation_detail: Trained on binary CIFAR clean data augmented with 8,000 randomly labeled examples; test accuracy reported at the selected stopping point.
rows.uncertainty: Results aggregated over 5 seeds (Fig. 1); uncertainty interval not stated.
rows.note: Table 1 gives test accuracy and predicted accuracy bound for multiclass CIFAR10, whereas this row concerns binary CIFAR. The paper reports the binary CIFAR result only in Fig. 1, without a numerical value in the text.
rows.check: 54.2% belongs to the multiclass CIFAR-10 MLP in Table 1, already recorded in R7. Remove that value from this binary CIFAR row and change its locator to Fig. 1. The supplied figure text does not establish a numerical architecture comparison. Architecture depth is inconsistent in the source: Section 5 says five layers, whereas Appendix C.2 says four.

rows.subject: ResNet

rows.uncertainty: Results aggregated over 5 seeds (Fig. 1); uncertainty interval not stated.
rows.note: The paper says the bounds closely track clean population accuracy; precise test-accuracy values are not stated in text.
rows.check: Relevant architecture counterpart to R1, but the supplied figure text does not establish the test-accuracy difference. Fig. 1 reports trajectories rather than an explicitly identified selected stopping-point value.

rows.subject: 2-layer wide network
rows.size_stated: 200000 hidden units; also tested with second layer fixed at random initialization and with both layers updated
rows.operation_detail: Added randomly labeled training examples and trained with SGD on MSE without early stopping or weight decay.
rows.value: Adding extra randomly labeled data hurts the unseen clean performance.
rows.uncertainty: Results aggregated over 3 seeds (Fig. 2); uncertainty interval not stated.
rows.note: The text states the direction of the effect but gives no numeric test-performance values.
rows.check: The random-label addition penalty measures none of V1–V8; partial is therefore inappropriate as a version-relative state. Fig. 2(b) sweeps the random-label fraction rather than reporting only 20%; Appendix C.4 inconsistently describes a fixed 20% setting.

rows.subject: 2-layer wide network
rows.size_stated: 200000 hidden units; also tested with second layer fixed at random initialization and with both layers updated
rows.operation_detail: Added randomly labeled training examples and used early stopping or weight decay instead of training to interpolation.
rows.measure: difference in unseen clean performance with additional randomly labeled data
rows.uncertainty: Results aggregated over 3 seeds (Fig. 2); uncertainty interval not stated.
rows.note: Authors also report tight bounds on unseen clean accuracy with these settings.
rows.check: Early stopping and weight decay are not dropout interventions and do not test V6. The reported near-zero penalty is valid for the separate noise-addition finding. Split the two interventions if retaining detailed results; Fig. 2(b) sweeps the random-label fraction.

rows.subject: MLP
rows.operation_detail: Trained on clean data augmented with randomly labeled data; reported test accuracy and RATT predicted accuracy bound.
rows.note: The table also reports predicted accuracy 93.1 and best accuracy 97.9; the text says all four settings had non-vacuous bounds and the gap between best and test accuracy was small.
rows.check: Use R6 as the architecture comparator: MLP accuracy is 97.4%, versus ResNet's 98.8%. Add the shared momentum 0.9 and weight decay 5 × 10⁻⁴ conditions. Table 1's 93.1 predicted accuracy is only the dominating term; the full bound subtracts another 30.7 percentage points.
